name: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques
text:
# Interpolation and Sampling Techniques

Also called: Trilinear Interpolation (DRR), Trilinear rendering

## Overview
This family defines how discrete voxel data is converted into continuous scalar values for [direct volume ray casting](#19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md]. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (aliasing, blockiness) inherent in [nearest-neighbor sampling](#11694-nearest-neighbor-sampling.md) by providing spatial reconstruction kernels and sampling strategies that balance computational cost against spatial smoothness [S2, unofficial][S3]. It sets itself apart from sibling techniques like [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md) by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel rather than the temporal or positional jittering of sample points, and from [Gradient-Based Interpolation by Sample Splatting](9072-gradient-based-interpolation-by-sample-splatting.md) by typically operating directly on the voxel grid rather than sparse sample splats.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family map a query position $\mathbf{p}$ in [voxel space](#3074-voxel-space.md) to a scalar value $V(\mathbf{p})$ by combining a finite set of neighboring voxel values $V_i$ using a set of weights $w_i(\mathbf{p})$:
$$
V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum_{i} w_i(\mathbf{p}) V_i
$$
The weights are derived from a reconstruction kernel $h(\mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{z}$ is the distance from the query point to the sample center [G]. The choice of kernel defines the trade-off between computational complexity, spatial extent (number of neighbors), and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring) [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Depth to Distance Conversion](2428-depth-to-distance-conversion.md)
Transforms discrete depth samples ($z\_vals$) along a ray into physical segment lengths ($dists$) required for volume rendering integration. It solves the problem that raw depth differences do not represent true Euclidean distances when the ray is not aligned with the viewing direction. It differs from [NDC Points to Distance](2500-ndc-points-to-distance.md) by operating in [camera-space depth](#5665-depth-from-ray-distance.md) coordinates rather than [Normalized Device Coordinates](#842-ndc-ray-reparameterization.md), making it suitable for standard perspective projection pipelines where depth is linear in camera space but non-linear in screen space.

### [Alpha Grid Mask](2430-alpha-grid-mask.md)
A module that stores a 3D alpha volume and provides efficient sampling of alpha values at arbitrary 3D coordinates using trilinear interpolation. It serves as the core sampling primitive for volume rendering to incorporate spatially varying opacity constraints derived from external supervision or geometry masks.

### [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md)
A [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) technique that casts rays from the camera through a 3D voxel grid, samples voxel data with jittered step offsets to reduce banding artifacts, and composites the result using front-to-back [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md). It perturbs sample positions along each ray using a pre-computed jitter texture to break up [regular grid](#3950-regular-grid.md) patterns.

### [Slab-based Ray Sampling](2853-slab-based-ray-sampling.md)
An [image-order caching](#2853-slab-based-ray-sampling.md) mechanism for direct volume ray casting that groups rays into rectangular screen regions to build stacked slabs reaching into the scene. Unlike object-order [bricking](#914-bricking.md), which relies on per-brick lists inefficient for GPU hardware, this method stores voxel sampling results in a regular three-dimensional array in shared memory, optimizing memory bandwidth and latency for lighting techniques that require neighborhood access, such as gradient calculation or ambient occlusion.

### [Epipolar Sampling](3899-epipolar-sampling.md)
A technique for aggregating features from multiple views by sampling along epipolar lines rather than along camera rays in 3D space. It solves the problem of efficiently correlating information between a reference view and target views without performing full 3D volume rendering or explicit 3D reconstruction during the encoding phase. Unlike [standard volume rendering](#1165-standard-volume-rendering-equation.md) which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. This allows the encoder to memorize the correct depth consistent with the scene's arbitrary scale, which is then used for subsequent parameter prediction.

### [Hierarchical Sampling](4865-hierarchical-sampling.md)
A two-stage sampling strategy used in [neural volume rendering](#1576-neural-volume-rendering.md) (specifically [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)) to improve rendering quality and efficiency by concentrating samples in regions of high geometric or radiance complexity. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling, where many samples fall in empty space or smooth regions, by using a coarse network to estimate the density distribution and then [importance-sampling](#9521-importance-sampling.md) along the ray based on that estimate. It sets itself apart from standard direct volume ray casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md] by replacing uniform discretization with a learned, non-uniform probability density function (PDF) derived from a separate coarse model, and from [Neural volume rendering](1576-neural-volume-rendering.md) by explicitly decoupling the density estimation (coarse) from the final color prediction (fine) into two distinct passes.

### [Space Warping (Log+Warp)](5815-space-warping-log-warp.md)
A [positional encoding](#876-positional-encoding.md) strategy for [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) that warps 3D space towards the view cell center using radial distortion. It solves the problem of high-frequency background details requiring excessive network capacity by dampening these frequencies while preserving foreground detail. It sets itself apart from standard [logarithmic sampling](#5814-non-linear-logarithmic-sampling.md) by applying an additional inverse-square-root warp to the encoded coordinates, ensuring that sample locations in space remain consistent across different viewpoints.

### [MLS Volume Reconstruction](9796-mls-volume-reconstruction.md)
A volume rendering technique that reconstructs a smooth scalar field from discrete samples (regular or irregular grids) using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation, allowing for adaptive preintegration to handle the computational cost of the scalar field evaluation. Unlike Radial Basis Functions (RBFs), which require solving a global system of equations, MLS solves a local weighted least squares problem at each query point, making it more efficient for large datasets. It provides a unifying framework that subsumes convolution (equivalent to MLS with a constant basis) and allows for tunable smoothing and interpolation control.

### [Interpolation Methods](10526-interpolation-methods.md)
[Interpolation methods](#10526-interpolation-methods.md) reconstruct a continuous scalar field from discrete voxel data to evaluate density or opacity at arbitrary query positions along viewing rays [G]. This family solves the problem of discretization artifacts (aliasing, blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling while balancing computational cost against spatial smoothness. It sets itself apart from sibling techniques like [Sampling and Jittering](2516-sampling-and-jittering.md) by focusing on the spatial reconstruction kernel rather than the temporal or positional jittering of sample points, and from [Gradient-Based Interpolation by Sample Splatting](9072-gradient-based-interpolation-by-sample-splatting.md) by typically operating directly on the voxel grid rather than sparse sample splats.

### Svox1 Rendering Formula (Nearest-Neighbor)
Implements the Svox1 rendering formula using [nearest-neighbor interpolation](#5891-nearest-neighbor-interpolation.md) with infinitely many steps. Includes forward, backward, and fused variants [S2, unofficial].
Code: `Tensor volume_render_svox1(SparseGridSpec &, RaysSpec &, RenderOptions &); void volume_render_svox1_backward(SparseGridSpec &, RaysSpec &, RenderOptions &, Tensor, Tensor, GridOutputGrads &); void volume_render_svox1_fused(SparseGridSpec &, RaysSpec &, RenderOptions &, Tensor, float, float, Tensor, GridOutputGrads &);` [S2, unofficial].

### Space-covering volume sampling
A technique to extend [pre-integrated volume rendering](#5327-pre-integrated-volume-rendering.md) to multidimensional transfer functions [S3].

## Background
Trilinear interpolation is a standard technique for generating Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRR) that samples voxel densities along rays, offering a speed advantage over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method [S1, unofficial]. Siddon's method computes exact intersections of every cast ray with voxels, taking ~25 ms for a standard AP view, while trilinear interpolation takes ~737 μs with 25 points [S1, unofficial]. The rendering cost of trilinear interpolation matches Siddon's method when the number of sample points ($n\_points$) is about 2,000 [S1, unofficial]. Performance benchmarks for trilinear interpolation with $n\_points=25$ is 737 μs ± 2.87 μs; with $n\_points=50$ is 1.03 ms ± 1.23 μs; with $n\_points=100$ is 1.65 ms ± 812 ns; with $n\_points=200$ is 3.52 ms ± 3.84 μs; with $n\_points=250$ is 4.75 ms ± 5.13 μs; with $n\_points=500$ is 7.63 ms ± 935 ns; with $n\_points=1000$ is 13.1 ms ± 4.73 μs; with $n\_points=2000$ is 25 ms ± 7.9 μs; with $n\_points=2500$ is 32.3 ms ± 10.8 μs; with $n\_points=3750$ is 48 ms ± 11 μs; with $n\_points=5000$ is 66 ms ± 11.1 μs [S1, unofficial].
